question: What do we call a sudden poisoning that happens right after a person has one large exposure to a chemical?
explanation: You've got this! Acute exposure simply means a one-time, short contact with a substance that quickly leads to symptoms or harm. Think of it as a sudden event, unlike chronic exposure which builds up over a long time. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h1)

question: When someone breathes in gases or vapors, why do they get absorbed into the body so quickly?

options.A: Inhaled toxins always bypass the liver completely
options.B: The skin blocks all other forms of chemical entry
options.C: The stomach acid breaks down inhaled chemicals instantly
options.D: The lungs have a large surface area and a rich blood supply

explanation: Great clinical thinking! The tiny air sacs (alveoli) in our lungs offer a massive surface area packed with blood vessels. This lets inhaled substances pass straight into the bloodstream without wasting any time. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h1)

question: In many Nigerian homes, what hazardous substance is most commonly swallowed by young children by accident because it was stored in an empty soft drink bottle?
explanation: Spot on! Kerosene is widely used for cooking and lighting. When poured into empty soft drink bottles, kids easily mistake it for a drink and swallow it. Always remember to teach parents to use proper, labeled containers! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h2)

question: A farmer comes to the clinic drooling, crying watery tears, and having muscle twitching after spraying his crops. Which type of chemical is most likely to blame?
explanation: Well done! Organophosphates overstimulate the nervous system by blocking an enzyme called acetylcholinesterase. This creates those classic 'wet' signs like drooling, excessive tearing, and twitching. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h2)

question: When trying to keep people safe from chemicals at work, what is considered the absolute best first step?

options.A: Conducting weekly medical tests on every worker
options.B: Handing out expensive protective gear to all staff
options.C: Putting warning signs on every single office door
options.D: Replacing a toxic chemical with a safer alternative

explanation: Brilliant! Substituting a dangerous chemical with a safer one completely removes the hazard instead of just managing the risk. Elimination is always the gold standard in safety. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h3)

question: Why is eating or drinking inside a chemical storage room a major safety violation?

options.A: It creates a direct pathway for hand-to-mouth chemical ingestion
options.B: It attracts pests that chew through the chemical packaging
options.C: Digestion slows down significantly in cold storage rooms
options.D: Food particles will ruin the chemical composition of stored products

explanation: Exactly right! Invisible chemical residues can settle on your hands, food, or drinks, making it super easy to swallow them by accident. Always keep food and drinks well away from chemicals! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h3)

question: What is the biggest danger of pouring leftover chemicals into empty beverage bottles?

options.A: The chemical instantly turns into a harmless gas
options.B: Labels become permanently stamped into the plastic
options.C: People may accidentally drink the toxic chemical
options.D: The plastic material dissolves within a few hours

explanation: You got it! Putting chemicals in drink bottles is a recipe for disaster because it tricks anyone—especially thirsty children—into thinking it's safe juice or water. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h4)

question: Why must acids and alkaline substances (bases) never be stored right next to each other?

options.A: Mixing them can cause violent reactions, heat, or toxic gas
options.B: Alkaline fumes destroy the paper labels on acid containers
options.C: They will neutralize each other and become expensive perfume
options.D: Acids make alkaline bottles shrink and leak everywhere

explanation: Spot on! Acids and bases react strongly when they meet, often releasing dangerous heat, splashes, or poisonous fumes. Keeping them apart keeps everyone safe. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h4)

question: Where does Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) fit into the safety hierarchy for handling workplace hazards?

options.A: It is the last line of defense after other controls
options.B: It is only required after a toxic exposure has occurred
options.C: It replaces the need for proper chemical labelling
options.D: It is the primary method to eliminate workplace hazards

explanation: That's correct! PPE depends entirely on human behavior and proper wear, making it our last safety net if other controls fail. We always prefer removing the danger first. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h5)

question: Which of the following is a WRONG practice when using chemical safety gloves?

options.A: Wearing the exact same pair of gloves indefinitely without checking them
options.B: Inspecting the glove material for tears before starting work
options.C: Washing hands thoroughly after safely removing the gloves
options.D: Choosing glove material resistant to the specific chemical used

explanation: Well reasoned! Gloves wear out, tear, and let chemicals soak through over time. You must check them often and replace them regularly—never wear the same pair forever! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h5)

question: If someone accidentally gets a corrosive chemical in their eyes or on their skin, what is the recommended minimum time to flush it with clean water?
explanation: You nailed it! Flushing continuously for at least 15 minutes is crucial to dilute the chemical and wash it away before it burns deep into the tissue. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h6)

question: Why should you never make a patient vomit after they have swallowed a strong acid?

options.A: It forces the acid to enter the bloodstream through the lungs
options.B: It neutralizes the stomach acid so fast that the heart stops
options.C: It prevents medical personnel from ever identifying the poison
options.D: It causes the corrosive chemical to damage the esophagus a second time

explanation: Excellent clinical instinct! Bringing the acid back up forces it to burn the delicate lining of the throat and mouth all over again, making the injury much worse. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h6)

question: What is the main goal of community nursing surveillance when it comes to poisons and toxic substances?

options.A: To replace the need for community health education
options.B: To detect patterns or outbreaks of poisoning early
options.C: To calculate the exact financial cost of chemical imports
options.D: To punish factories that fail safety inspections

explanation: Spot on! Tracking poison cases helps public health teams spot trends quickly, allowing us to step in and save lives before more people get hurt. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h7)

question: A community health nurse notices several children from different families coming in with the exact same pesticide poisoning signs. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Advise the local schools to close down all science laboratories
options.B: Treat the children and assume it is an isolated domestic accident
options.C: Wait until the end of the year to write a formal summary report
options.D: Report the cluster to public health authorities for investigation

explanation: You've got it! When multiple cases point to a shared source, alerting public health authorities right away helps track down the cause and protect the whole neighborhood. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h7)
